summaries.summary: Sarcasm is an intensive, indirect, complex construct often expressing contempt or ridicule, and textual sarcasm lacks non-linguistic modalities, making recognition challenging for humans and machines.

Sarcasm detection is indispensable for online review summarizers, dialog systems, recommendation systems and sentiment analyzers, but traditional NLP tools and techniques have struggled, as DBLP:journals/corr/JoshiBC16 reports.
A sarcastic movie review about theater air conditioning illustrates why automatic sentiment analyzers need information beyond textual analysis to infer negative sentiment toward the movie.

The authors exploit psycholinguistic sarcasm detection using cognitive features from eye-tracking, motivated by distinctive eye movement patterns when reading sarcastic texts compared with literal texts.

Cognitive features and textual features from best available sarcasm detectors train binary classifiers against sarcasm labels, significantly improving classification accuracy over the state of the art.
Prior research defines sarcasm through figurative opposition, pretense, indirect negation, and a six tuple entity, with ivanko2003context studying cognitive aspects of sarcasm processing.
Computational linguists used rule based and statistical techniques with Unigrams and Pragmatic features, Stylistic patterns, situational disparity patterns, and Hastag interpretations.
Most prior sarcasm detection uses distant supervision and stylistic/pragmatic features, but linguistically well-formed structures without explicit cues remain hard using such features alone.

Eye-trackers and EEG/MEG devices enabled cognitive studies, including Filik2014, Camblin2007103, and BIBREF8 augmenting eye-movement cognitive features with textual features to detect realized sarcasm.
Recent literature motivates exploring gaze-based cognition for sarcasm detection, which the authors describe as the first work of its kind.

Sarcasm emanates from incongruity, causing reanalysis and distinctive eye-movement patterns, a hypothesis validated using the previously released freely available sarcasm dataset BIBREF8 enriched with gaze information.
The database contains 1,000 short texts of 10-40 words, including 350 sarcastic texts and 650 non-sarcastic texts, with normalized tweets and aspect-specific positive or negative opinions.
Seven graduate students with science and engineering backgrounds and good English proficiency received instructions about the task, annotation input method, and minimizing head movement.
Annotators read sentences and assigned binary polarity labels, not sarcasm labels, to avoid the Priming Effect and preserve ecological validity by mixing sarcastic and non sarcastic text.
An SR-Research Eyelink-1000 eye-tracker in monocular remote mode at 500Hz recorded fixations, saccade and pupil size while readers saw one sentence and its aspect.
Polarity annotation accuracy varied between 72%-91% for sarcastic texts and 75%-91% for non-sarcastic text, with errors attributed to attention, comprehension, and lack of context.

Incorrect annotations are retained because online readers cannot be segregated, assuming most readers identify sarcasm and averaged eye-movement parameters remain undistorted for regular and multi-instance based classifiers.
Distinct behavior during sarcasm reading is observed by analyzing “fixation duration on the text”, also called “dwell time”, and readers' “scanpaths”.
Average fixation duration per word is at least 1.5 times higher for sarcastic texts, and a two-tailed t-test with INLINEFORM0 set to 0.05 shows significant differences for all participants.
Longer fixations may reflect other linguistic subtleties or occulomotor control problems, but sarcasm label was the most significant predictor with a maximum slope in a linear mixed effect model.
The authors now analyze scanpaths to gain more insights into the sarcasm comprehension process.
Scanpaths are line-graphs with fixations as nodes and saccades as edges, with Figure FIGREF14 showing three participants' scanpaths for sarcastic sentence S1 and non-sarcastic sentence S2.

Qualitative scanpath-analysis reveals long regressions and higher fixation durations on incongruous phrases A and B, seen in S1 for “misconception”, “cherish”, “always cherish” and “original misconception”, but not S2.
Distinctive scanpaths do not guarantee sarcasm because literal texts may show them, so linguistic features, readability and scanpath-derived features may help discriminative machine learning models.

Features in Table include lexical, implicit incongruity and explicit incongruity features borrowed mainly from joshi2015harnessing, plus readability and word count to reduce text hardness and length effects.

Simple gaze based features quantify fixations, forward saccades, skips and regressions through statistical aggregation or multi-instance based learning, and are introduced to NLP tasks like textual sarcasm detection for the first time.
Complex gaze based features rely on a graph structure called “saliency graphs”, derived from eye-gaze information and word sequences in the text.
For each reader and sentence, a “saliency graph” INLINEFORM2 has vertices INLINEFORM3 and edges INLINEFORM4, with vertices corresponding to words and edges to at least one saccade.
Figure FIGREF15 shows a saliency graph that may be weighted but not necessarily connected, with complex gaze features motivated by incongruity, including Edge Density and highest weighted degree.

Sarcasm detection is binary classification using 994 examples from the eye-movement database, stratified 10-fold cross validation, comparisons with riloff2013sarcasm and joshi2015harnessing, and Weka BIBREF18 and LibSVM BIBREF19 APIs.
Table TABREF17 shows classification results considering various feature combinations for different classifiers and other systems.
Unigram uses principal components of unigram feature vectors.
Sarcasm is the feature-set reported by joshi2015harnessing, subsuming unigram features and features from other reported systems.
Gaze is the simple and complex cognitive features introduced by the authors, along with readability and word count features.
Gaze+Sarcasm is the complete set of features.
Regular classifiers average gaze features across participants, while MILR forms a multi instance “bag” from each participant's gaze features and linguistic features for each sentence.

All classifiers with the feature combination outperform unigram baselines and BIBREF3, with MILR gaining 3.7% F-score and 0.08 Kappa, SVM improving 2%, and gaze alone showing high-precision but low recall.

A McNemar test comparing joshi2015harnessing linguistic features with MILR using complete features found significant accuracy difference with p(two-tailed) = 0.02 and odds-ratio of 1.43 in a 95% confidence interval.

Using “reading time” as the only cognitive feature with textual features yields F-scores close to sarcasm features alone, with no statistically significant improvement, while gaze features are superior.

Cognitive feature effectiveness is examined with a stratified 80%:20% train-test split and training on 100%, 90%, 80% and 70% of training data, showing F-score and Kappa improvements in Figure FIGREF22.
Chi squared test and Information Gain test rank 16 out of top 20 features as gaze features, with Average Fixation Duration per Word and Largest Regression Position most significant.
Table TABREF21 shows example cases from the experiment with stratified 80%-20% train-test split.
Example sentence 1 is sarcastic, requires extra-linguistic knowledge about poor living conditions at Manchester, and our system predicts successfully, possibly helped by gaze features.
For sentence 2, phrases like “Helped me” and “Can't stop” affect the linguistic-only system, while our system performs well.
Sentence 3 is a false-negative case where humans struggled, and gaze features and the complete set of features account for erroneous prediction.
In sentence 4, gaze features alone false-indicate incongruity, whereas the system predicts correctly with gaze and linguistic features together.
These examples imply that only gaze features would not suffice to rule out detecting other forms of incongruity that do not result in sarcasm.
System errors arise from eye-tracker hardware limitations, linguistic tools and resources errors, and possible information loss from aggregating eye-tracking parameters.
The novel framework augments linguistic features with cognitive gaze-based and graph-derived features, improving sarcasm detector success rate by 3.7% over the best available system.

The general approach may aid sentiment and emotion analysis, text summarization and question answering, with future work on deeper graph and gaze features and complex gaze feature representation models.
We thank CFILT Lab members, especially Jaya Jha and Meghna Singh, and IIT Bombay students for their help and support.
